cells.tense: You're seeing what's actually there in front of you, right now, without adding to it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you can see clearly about what you're growing — say it out loud to yourself before the day starts.
cells.core:
You're seeing what's in front of you — the actual shape of the thing, not what you hope it is or worry it might be. When you tend what's growing, you don't force it. You look, you notice what it needs, you give that. That kind of sight doesn't come from trying harder. It comes from being willing to see what's there before deciding what to do about it.

What you're looking at is early — a first cut, not a finished picture. There's no proof yet that it'll work, and you're not asking for proof. You watch closely enough to respond to what's actually happening instead of what you planned. That's the balance. It's not passive. It's the kind of attention that lets something become what it is. You keep that by leaving room for the thing to surprise you. Keep looking before you know.
cells.sheetLine: You see what's there before you decide what to do.
cells.verb: seeing the first clear shape of what's growing, before it has a name
cells.place: in the quiet where something small is being tended until it can stand

cells.tense: You'll be watching for what could go wrong before it has a chance to happen.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're growing and don't check on it today — let it have one unobserved day.
cells.core:
You're seeing problems before they exist. Something's growing and you're already ahead of it, spotting what might fail, what needs fixing, what could go sideways. What you notice is real — you're not imagining the risks — but you're using it like a shield against a future that hasn't arrived. The care turns into vigilance. The vigilance turns into control. And the thing you're trying to protect gets less room to grow because you're standing over it.

The first cut of clarity is supposed to be simple — just what's there. Not predicting. Not defending. Not managing. You can still see clearly without acting on everything you see. The ask isn't to stop noticing. It's to let one thing alone for a day, so it can show you what it becomes when you're not braced for its failure.
cells.sheetLine: You're watching so hard the thing can't grow.

cells.tense: You stopped looking closely at what you were growing, and you haven't picked it back up.
cells.ask: Set a timer for five minutes and look at one thing you're growing — just look, no fixing, and write down one thing you notice.
cells.core:
The looking went quiet. Something you were tending stopped getting your attention, and you're not sure when that happened. It's not that you stopped caring. It's that looking got harder and you stopped trusting it, or someone else's view crowded yours out, and now you're going through the motions without actually seeing what's in front of you.

Clear sight starts small — one true look, nothing more. Not a plan. Not a fix. Just one real thing about what's growing. You don't have to feel inspired. You don't have to know what it means. You just have to look at it for five minutes, without the pressure to make anything happen. It's still there to be picked up. The picking up is what's been on hold.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped looking, and the not-looking became the habit.

cells.tense: You're already seeing what needs tending, and you're calling it something else.
cells.ask: Next time you notice something about what's growing, say 'I noticed that' instead of 'it just happened' or 'it seemed obvious.'
cells.core:
You're already reading the room. You know what's off before anyone says it. You know what a thing needs before it asks. But you don't call it noticing — you say you're just being practical, or paying attention, or nothing special. You name it circumstance or common sense while it guides what you do all day.

That's not humility. It's a kind of disappearance. You're the one doing the looking, and you've been talking like the looking happens by itself. Naming it — just saying 'I noticed that' when you notice something — doesn't make you arrogant. It makes you accurate about where it comes from. And when you own it, you can trust it on purpose instead of only when it sneaks up on you.
cells.sheetLine: You're already seeing it. You just won't say so.

attempts.check: The record doesn't support 'you've always been the patient one' or any history in this seat — especially in Too Little, where I can say the tending went quiet but not who stopped needing it or how long it's been. The reader might say 'I'm not avoiding anything, people just don't listen' — and the ask still works, because naming one thing doesn't require them to agree with my read. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you were born to nurture' — that's flattery, not the map.
